there are 13 distinct regimes of spreading for an elastic sheet driven by gravity and viscous resistance, depending on the relative strengths of bending, tension and gravity, the two-dimensional or axisymmetric geometry and whether the effects of fluid inertia, surface tension and fluid viscosity at the front are included.

the fluid front moves at a speed that depends on the ratio of the length scale of the system to three key transition length scale, namely the viscous length scale, the bending length scale and the tension length scale.
the blister of viscous fluid under an elastic sheet spreads at a constant rate that is proportional to the bending modulus, the elastic tension and the viscosity of the fluid.

the dynamics of fluid under an elastic sheet and the resulting fluid spreading, and we have shown how to use matched asymptotic expansions in order to obtain a detailed description of the spreading behaviour.

the spreading dynamics of a viscous fluid under a deformable elastic sheet are extremely complicated, and the present paper should be regarded as a first step in a long-term program of research.

the spreading rate of a blister of fluid is governed by the relative strength of the three driving mechanisms, and that this relative strength is determined by the horizontal length scale of the system, the thickness of the elastic sheet and the viscosity of the injected fluid.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fluid spreads outwards at a rate that increases as the inverse of the square root of time, with a profile that decays exponentially in the radial direction.

the spreading rate and profile of a viscous fluid injected into an elastic sheet is determined by the relative importance of gravity and elastic bending and tension effects, and by the relative importance or otherwise of the effects of inertia and surface tension.
there are at least 17 different asymptotic regimes in which the blister can spread.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for any given system, the spreading behaviour is determined by the relative strengths of the forces acting on the system, and not by the precise details of the geometry.
the blister spreading rate and thickness are controlled by the bending force on small scales and the gravity force on large scales.
